question: Where must a this(...) constructor delegation call appear inside a constructor body?

options.text: Anywhere in the constructor provided super(...) was called first.
As the very first statement in the constructor body.
Immediately following parameter validation and range check statements.
At the end of the constructor body just before returning.

explanation: The Java language specification mandates that any explicit constructor invocation via this(...) must be the first statement in the constructor body. Placing statements before this(...) causes a compilation error.

question: How many explicit this(...) constructor delegation calls can a single constructor body contain?

options.text: Any number of calls is allowed as long as they appear after validation.
Multiple calls are permitted provided each initializes a distinct field.
At most one, and it must appear as the first statement.
Two calls are permitted if one delegates to super(...) first.

explanation: A constructor can delegate to at most one other constructor using this(...). Multiple this(...) calls in a single constructor body are illegal because only the first statement can be an explicit constructor invocation.

question: Can a single constructor body explicitly invoke both super(...) and this(...)?

options.text: Yes, provided the class extends an abstract superclass.
No, because both calls require being the first statement, so at most one is allowed.
Yes, as long as super(...) is written before this(...).
Yes, if super(...) handles fields and this(...) handles methods.

explanation: Java allows at most one explicit constructor invocation statement in a constructor, and it must be the first statement. A constructor cannot contain both super(...) and this(...) because only one can occupy the first position.

question: What does the Java compiler do if two constructors in the same class delegate to each other in a circular loop?

options.text: It allows the compilation but throws StackOverflowError upon program execution.
It permits the loop and resolves recursion dynamically via stack unwinding.
It automatically breaks the loop by injecting super() before the second delegation.
It catches the circularity at compile time and rejects it as a recursive constructor invocation error.

explanation: The Java compiler performs static analysis to detect cycles in constructor chaining. If constructors recursively delegate to each other, javac rejects the program with: recursive constructor invocation.
